message.content: {"bid_amount":38,"public_message":"38.","private_thought":"Stay in. Marvin mortgage is $140; a win at \u2264$89 leaves \u2265$150 after mortgage so I can 4/4/4 LB ($400/$400/$450) before p1 acts. p1 winning cheap is worst: $37 + mortgage funds Indiana to 2h. I can only bid to $99, so rational p1 outbids and still builds \u2014 then push price to drain their cushion. Do not drop before $99. Do not fund anyone. Houses left: 5; I need 3."}
message.reasoning:
I need to decide on an auction bid for Marvin Gardens.

I have $99 cash and a strong light-blue monopoly with three houses each. The current high bid is $37, so the minimum next bid is $38. I am weighing whether to outbid p1 or drop out.

The yellow monopoly is split. I own Ventnor Avenue and p3 owns Atlantic Avenue. The auction for Marvin Gardens is unowned.

No one can form a yellow monopoly yet. I would own Ventnor and Marvin, but Atlantic remains with p3. A win at $89 or less leaves enough cash to mortgage the property and still have over $150 afterward. This makes the auction worthwhile.

A bid of $35 would leave p1 with enough cash to mortgage and fund an Indiana house. I should not drop out or fund anyone.

Marvin Gardens has a $140 mortgage value, so buying it for $99 or less would yield a net profit of $140 minus the purchase price. The key question is whether any rent is due before my turn.

The auction began on p2's turn. A win at $89 or less leaves enough cash to mortgage the property and fund fourth houses on the light-blue set.

A $38 bid leaves $61 cash, which mortgages to $201. That covers the $150 needed for fourth houses on the light-blue set and leaves a $51 surplus.

The key question is whether I can mortgage immediately after winning the auction or only on my own turn. The auction is currently running during p2's turn, so I need to determine whose turn follows p2.

The turn history is confusing. p4 appears to have ended its turn twice in a row, and p2 seems to have started the auction immediately after ending its own turn. This suggests the turn indices may not match the actual player order.

The auction is still running during p2's turn. Play resumes with p3, then p4, so I cannot mortgage Marvin until my next turn. p3 is on CHANCE with no cash and may move before then. No rent is due from me until I roll.

Owning Marvin carries no rent risk until I land on it. A $38 bid leaves $61 cash, which is sufficient for the mortgage when my turn arrives. p1 has $138 and could outbid me, but that would still yield a $140 mortgage profit.

p1 cannot afford a fourth house on the red set. They are short $12 and in jail, so buying Marvin would waste cash they need to build. I should bid to deny them that arbitrage.

A $128 bid would leave p1 with exactly $150 after mortgaging Marvin, allowing them to build a house. Since they only have $138, they cannot afford that high a bid.

I cannot bid $138 because p1 would outbid me at $139, and I only have $99. A $99 win leaves me with zero cash, but mortgaging Marvin for $140 on my next turn gives a net gain of $41.

I cannot force p1 above $128 with a $99 bid. They can always outbid me and still afford a house after mortgaging. I am now weighing whether to keep bidding to extract more cash or drop out.

A $37 win leaves p1 with $101. Mortgaging Marvin for $140 gives them $241, enough to build one Indiana house and reach even development at 2/2/2. They cannot afford a second house. Standard red monopoly rent is $36/$36/$40.

Red monopoly rent with two houses is $250/$250/$300. Indiana's rent would jump from $90 to $250 if p1 builds there. A $100 win leaves p1 with $28 cash versus $91, but the strategic outcome is identical.

A $37 win leaves p1 with $101 cash. After paying the $50 jail fee, they would have $51. They cannot mortgage Marvin until their own turn. The turn order is p3, then p4, then p1.

I will mortgage Marvin on my turn if I win, before p1 moves. If p1 wins, they mortgage it after me. The light-blue set is fully developed at three houses each, yielding $270/$270/$300 in rent. A $50 jail fee would let p1 roll and land on those properties. I am now weighing whether to drop out and let p1 take the property for $37.

I am now considering whether to keep bidding to drain p1's cash. If I bid $99, they would outbid me at $100 and still afford a house after mortgaging. A tighter bid leaves them with only $28 cash afterward. I am wondering if p1 might not outbid me at all.

p1 is matching my bids incrementally, so they are actively contesting the auction. They may want the property for its mortgage value, to block a yellow monopoly, or simply to compete. I am now weighing whether to drop out and let them secure a $37 bargain, or push the bid higher to extract more cash from them.

p1 cannot afford a house without mortgaging Marvin. Their $138 is exactly $12 short of the $150 needed for one house, so they must mortgage to build this turn. This makes the auction outcome critical for their development plans.

p1 has no other mortgageable assets. Their red properties are all mortgaged and fully developed, so they cannot raise cash without selling or mortgaging them.

If p1 loses the auction, they remain at $138 and cannot build this turn. Indiana stays at one house with $90 rent, which is better for me than them winning and building.

If p1 wins, they can mortgage Marvin for $140 and afford a house after paying the bid.

A $138 bid would leave p1 with only $2 cash after mortgaging, so they cannot build and the purchase is nearly worthless to them. A $99 bid forces them to pay $100, which still nets them a $40 profit and the ability to build. They should take it. I cannot outbid them.

A $99 bid leaves p1 with $28 cash after mortgaging and building, making them vulnerable to my light-blue rent. A $37 win leaves them with $241, a much safer buffer. I am now weighing whether to push the price higher to drain their cash or drop out and let them secure the cheap property.

A $37 win leaves p1 with $91 cash after mortgaging. That is enough to survive a single light-blue rent of $270, but they would need to sell three red houses. A $99 win leaves them with only $28 cash. They would need to sell four houses to cover the same rent. The tighter bid would force them into bankruptcy.

I will keep bidding to drain p1's cash. Lower cash forces more house sales when they land on my light-blue set, weakening them. They cannot outbid me past roughly $128, so I will push the price as high as possible.

I will bid $38 to continue the auction. A $99 win leaves me with zero cash, but mortgaging Marvin on my next turn yields $140. That is $41 more than dropping out, and p1 cannot build a fourth house without the mortgage.

A $38 win leaves $61 cash, which plus the $140 mortgage gives $201. That is enough to build four houses and still have $51 left. A $99 win leaves only $10 cash, so the mortgage would cover exactly $150 and leave nothing for building. I will bid the minimum $38 to keep the option open, then escalate toward $89 or $99 if p1 keeps matching.

A $90 win leaves me $1 short of building four houses, while a $99 win leaves me $10 short. The light-blue set at four houses yields $400/$400/$450 in rent, making the property extremely valuable. I will bid the minimum $38 to keep the auction alive and avoid giving p1 an easy outbid.

Bidding $99 immediately would signal desperation and likely trigger a $100 counter-bid. A slow escalation to $89 or $99 is safer. p1's matching bids may be purely price-raising rather than a genuine desire for the property.

A $90 win would leave me with only $1 short of building four houses, but I would still net about $50 in cash and prevent p1 from developing. Bidding $89 would give me exactly enough for a full set. I will bid $38 to keep the auction alive, following the established pattern where I bid even numbers and p1 bids odd numbers.

I will bid $38 to keep the auction alive and avoid a bad price if p1 drops out. The bank has five houses and twelve hotels remaining, so I can build three more light-blue houses after mortgaging Marvin. I act before p1 in the turn order.

I will bid the minimum $38 to keep the auction alive. A higher bid would only accelerate an outbid without improving my expected outcome, since p1 cannot exceed roughly $128. I am also deciding whether to send a brief public message or stay silent.

I will keep the public message minimal to avoid revealing strategy. I am also noting that owning two of three yellow properties would complete a yellow monopoly.
